question_text: The Winstons released "Color Him Father" in 1969, and it won its writer a Grammy. The B-side hides a seven-second drum solo, named after the track it sits on. Those four bars, played alone by Gregory C. Coleman (the ___ break), have since become a kind of scripture: quoted more often than any other recording ever made, they power tracks by N.W.A, The Prodigy, David Bowie, Oasis, Nine Inch Nails and Slipknot, plus the Futurama theme, and whole genres, jungle and drum and bass among them, are built on nothing else. Despite all their prayers, The Winstons never received a penny, and Coleman died destitute in 2006. The break also shares its name with the most revered three-hole stretch in golf. Fill in the blank.

This film nearly didn't get finished at all. In 1998, someone clearing files typed rm -rf * one folder too high, and assets began vanishing from screens across the building. 90% of two years' work was gone, and the backups, it turned out, had been quietly failing for a month. The film survived because technical director Galyn Susman, working from home with a newborn, had a full copy on her own machine. By the time it was finished, a third of the team working on this film had some form of carpal tunnel syndrome or repetitive strain injury from being overworked. Which film are we talking about?

After being defeated by France in one of the qualifying rounds, the Dutch realized that weight was the critical issue. Roelof Klein and Francois Brandt decided that their regular third man not ideal for this event, and recruited a small local boy out of the crowd to take his place. They won. Olympic historians believe the boy was around eight years old when he participated in the 1900 Games, which would make him the youngest Olympic champion in history. The boy posed for a single photograph and vanished; nobody has ever identified him. Name the sport, and the role he filled.
answer_text: Rowing, the unknown boy coxswain. The coxed pair of 1900: believed to be the youngest Olympic champion ever, and the only one nobody has been able to name.

question_text: Connect (non-exhaustive): Cleave, Sanction, Dust, Oversight, Screen, Buckle.
answer_text: Contronyms (also called auto-antonyms or Janus words): cleave (split/cling), sanction (permit/penalise), dust (remove/apply), oversight (supervision/omission), screen (show/conceal), buckle (fasten/collapse).

question_text: Over the years X had gathered dust, dirt, and layer upon layer of varnish (applied by Y and by everyone who retouched it after him) until the whole scene had gone dim and yellow. That varnish saved it. In 1911 an unemployed shoemaker, furious at not finding work in the capital, attacked it with a knife: the coating was so thick the blade only scratched the surface. In 1939, as war approached, X was taken off its stretcher and moved ahead of the Wehrmacht from bunker to bunker until it ended up in a limestone cave vault a few miles from the German border, where it sat out the war. When conservators finally stripped the varnish afterwards, they found the scene had never been nocturnal: the shadows put it in the early afternoon. The name was a misnomer, and yet it stayed. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X - The Night Watch. Properly "Militia Company of District II under Captain Frans Banninck Cocq". Y - Rembrandt

question_text: It has been argued that Y owes rather more than a mood to X. Both X and Y begin at a comfortable desk, with a homebody who has no intention of going anywhere and an older companion who has other ideas. In both, the way in is a message in runes (hidden inside an old manuscript in X, hidden on an old map in Y) that nobody can read until the right person holds it up to the right light. In both, the message turns out to be an appointment: a portal into a subterranean domain unlocked when the star aligns, and both parties nearly miss it. Both send their traveller down into the belly of a mountain, past things that belong to a much older world, and bring him out the other side a transformed person. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X - Journey to the Centre of the Earth. Y - The Hobbit

question_text: X was first mentioned in writing in 1708, in a letter to Leibniz: a happy accident from a Berlin workshop where Diesbach had been trying to make cochineal red lake. X in its raw form is on the WHO's list of essential medicines. Odd, then, that if you break it down in a laboratory you get one of the most notorious poisons in chemistry, one that took its name from X. X was also famously used to depict a scene with three boats in a storm-tossed sea, with a mountain in the background. Identify X.

In the 2006 FA Cup final (remembered forever as the Gerrard final), a journeyman right-back on loan at West Ham burst down the flank and delivered the cross for the opening goal, though the man who actually put it in the net that day was Liverpool's Jamie Carragher. Twelve years later, handed a caretaker job nobody else wanted, he was dismissed by critics with the line that he "couldn't even direct traffic." He has since directed rather more than that, and, fittingly for a man who ended a near-endless thirty-six year wait, he shares his first name with the singer who soundtracked Endless Love and won an Oscar for White Nights. Identify him.
answer_text: Lionel Scaloni. Scaloni's cross forced Carragher's own goal in 2006; as Argentina's "traffic-directing" caretaker he won the 2021 Copa America, the 2022 World Cup and the 2024 Copa. The namesake: Lionel Richie.

question_text: A camel-hair brush is a type of paintbrush with soft bristles made from natural hairs, usually squirrel, ox or sable. In one instance, in the 1920s, these were used by young women, hired to paint numerals on Xs. However, the brushes would lose shape after a few strokes, so the supervisors encouraged their workers to shape the brushes' point with their lips ("lip, dip, paint") or use their tongues to keep them sharp. Some even painted their nails and teeth with it for fun. When the adverse effects began, the company's own consultants attributed it to syphilis. The landmark suit, brought by Grace Fryer and four co-workers against their New Jersey employer, helped establish an employee's right to sue for occupational disease. What is this group collectively called?
answer_text: The Radium Girls. Their bodies are still measurably radioactive. The standards they forced into law outlived every executive who lied to them.

question_text: Green Eggs and Ham reverses the traditional structure of an adult trying to convince a child to try new foods. It is one of many books written by X about a defiance of norms, in this case the persistence of Sam-I-am after his offer of green eggs and ham is rejected. It explores the underlying social connection between individuals set in opposition to one another, but it does so in a way that appeals to the interests of children. Both characters refuse to move from their decision throughout the book until the adult finally gives in at the end. X wrote the book after his editor bet him $50 that he could not write an engaging children's book under a certain condition. Give the condition/clause.
answer_text: Dr Seuss was challenged by Random House to write a children's book using at most 50 distinct words.

question_text: In the 1790s, it was decided that this unit should be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, which meant somebody had to go and measure it. Two astronomers spent seven years surveying the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona. One of them, checking his own Barcelona latitude readings, found a discrepancy he could not explain, hid it, and spent the rest of his life tormented by it, dying of fever in Spain in 1804 while trying to push the survey far enough south to bury the error. His partner Delambre found the doctored notebooks among his papers. The shortfall was never corrected, and is baked into the modern definition to this day. Which unit?
answer_text: The metre. Pierre Mechain's suppressed discrepancy: the metre is still about 0.2 mm short because of it.

question_text: The lowest-scoring game in the league's history, a 19-18 win for the Fort Wayne Pistons over the Minneapolis X on 22 November 1950, was less a contest than a hostage situation: the team in front simply kept possession, and as a result the crowd booed for most of the second half. The saviour turned out to be Danny Biasone, a bowling-alley owner who ran the Syracuse Nationals, and his fix was a piece of simple arithmetic. He went back through the games he'd actually enjoyed watching, and made an observation around what made them entertaining. In 1954 the league adopted his answer. What did Biasone's arithmetic produce? Also, identify X.
answer_text: The 24-second shot clock. 2,880 seconds divided by 120 shots equals 24. The clock saved the league from stall-ball. X - Lakers: Minneapolis Lakers now known as Los Angeles Lakers.

question_text: X was born in present-day Gdansk in 1686 and orphaned at fifteen when both his parents died on the same day after eating poisonous mushrooms; he ran away from a merchant's apprenticeship in Amsterdam, had a warrant issued for his arrest, spent years drifting around Europe as a glassblower, and was buried in a pauper's grave in The Hague. Y, born 44 miles north of Stockholm, into a family of scholars, spent a year in Lapland measuring the Earth to settle whether Newton was right about its shape, made more than three hundred observations of the aurora and was the first to link it to the Earth's magnetic field. Y was also one of the earliest to note that much of Scandinavia is slowly rising above sea level, postulating, incorrectly, that the water was draining away rather than the land coming up. It would not be the last time his work was flipped on its head. X and Y never met, and their fortunes could hardly have sat at more opposite ends of a scale, and yet are linked forever. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X = Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit; Y = Anders Celsius.

question_text: One of the few criticisms of this film was by Ziauddin Sardar, who noted that the film's two most prominent Muslim characters are reduced to weak stereotypes, one a buffoonish criminal, while the other is portrayed as an impotent victim. The original ending was supposed to be very different. The censors of a state that had just suspended civil liberties refused to let the film end with a citizen killing a man, however deserving, and a tamer one was hastily reshot. Identify this film loosely inspired by a Kurosawa classic.
answer_text: Sholay. Thakur crushing Gabbar with hobnailed sandals was reshot into a police rescue at the censors' insistence.

question_text: In May 1994 the government of Kiribati fell to a vote of no confidence, 19 votes to 21, and by the autumn a former schoolteacher named Teburoro Tito had won the presidency in a landslide, carrying a campaign promise that no leader anywhere had made before. Up until then, Kiribati was a country permanently at odds with itself and endured an administrative nightmare for two days of every week. On 1 January 1995 Tito kept his promise and resolved the issue once and for all. What did Tito do?
answer_text: It bent the International Date Line. Kiribati moved the line approximately 1,000 km east around the Line Islands, creating UTC+14, the furthest-forward time zone on Earth, and claiming the first sunrise of 2000.

question_text: Connect (non-exhaustive): 1945 - Carousel; 1945 - Frank Sinatra; 1963 - Ray Charles; 1963 - ____ and the ________; 1967 - Elvis Presley; 1972 - Aretha Franklin; 2003 - Johnny Cash, released two months after his death; 2023 - Marcus Mumford, over the closing scenes of the Ted Lasso finale.
answer_text: You'll Never Walk Alone. From Carousel (1945); Sinatra within months, Ray Charles on Ingredients in a Recipe for Soul, Elvis in '67, Aretha on Amazing Grace, Cash on the posthumous Unearthed, Mumford over Ted Lasso's finale and even Pink Floyd sampled this for Fearless (Meddle).
